source: Rips (2001) Two kinds of reasoning
finding: Rips gave two groups the same arguments. One group judged deductive correctness (necessary), the other inductive strength (plausible). He argued the order of arguments flipped between groups, so one shared strength scale with only a shifted cutoff could not explain it.
numbers: Psychological Science 12(2), 129-134. Numbers come from secondary reports (see a02, a03, a08).
limits: Journal page and abstract-level summary only; full text is paywalled, so not opened.
agent_relevance: Sets the paradigm: the only change is the question word, necessary versus plausible. The whole subfield reuses it.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: Describes the Rips (2001) crossover: under deduction, valid-but-unbelievable arguments were endorsed more than invalid-but-believable ones; under induction the order reversed. The authors say the pattern is close to a single dissociation and may fit one dimension.
numbers: As read by Hayes et al.: large valid-unbelievable minus invalid-believable gap under deduction, near zero gap under induction. A state-trace re-analysis of Rips data (Stephens et al.) was consistent with one dimension.
limits: Second-hand description of Rips, in a paper I read in full.
agent_relevance: The famous crossover may not be a true crossover. Do not use it as proof of two modes.

source: Heit & Rotello (2005) Are there two kinds of reasoning?
finding: Heit and Rotello name Rips' idea the criterion-shift account: one scale of argument strength, with a stricter cutoff for deductively valid than for inductively strong. Key prediction: the distance in d' between any two arguments should be the same under both instructions.
numbers: Instruction wording: deduction asks if the sentence below is necessarily true; induction asks if it is plausible. Three Rips wordings gave no differences, so one was used per condition.
limits: Quote: 'there is a stricter criterion for saying an argument is deductively correct as opposed to just inductively strong.'
agent_relevance: Gives a testable rule: if a validity check is only a stricter cutoff on the same signal, its accuracy equals the plausibility accuracy. The data say it did not.

source: Heit & Rotello (2005) Are there two kinds of reasoning?
finding: Experiment 1 (letters instead of meaning, so no background knowledge): deduction instructions separated correct from incorrect arguments much better than induction instructions. This is not a pure criterion shift.
numbers: N=40 per condition (Warwick undergraduates), 8 arguments (4 correct, 4 incorrect). Positive responses: deduction .89 correct, .22 incorrect; induction .93 correct, .55 incorrect. Mean d': deduction 1.68, induction 0.93, t(78)=3.11, p<.01. Interaction F(1,78)=9.67, p<.01.
limits: Small item set; between-subjects; conference paper.
agent_relevance: Valid items were accepted either way. The question wording mostly changed how many invalid items slipped through.

source: Heit & Rotello (2005) Are there two kinds of reasoning?
finding: Experiment 2 (category inclusion, e.g. all birds have C so all robins have C): same pattern. Correct arguments accepted about equally often; incorrect arguments accepted far more under induction.
numbers: N=48 per condition, 16 arguments. Correct: deduction .92, induction .88. Incorrect: deduction .24, induction .57. d': deduction 1.69, induction 0.78, t(94)=4.39, p<.001. Condition x correctness F(1,94)=19.22, p<.001. Typicality main effect F(1,94)=6.91, p<.01.
limits: Gaussian signal detection assumed; d' from overall proportions.
agent_relevance: A model told to judge plausibility will wave through invalid items that look typical.

source: Heit & Rotello (2005) Are there two kinds of reasoning?
finding: ROC curves built from 1-7 confidence ratings differed in height and slope between deduction and induction. Equal sensitivity with a shifted cutoff would give one shared line.
numbers: zROC slope Exp 1: deduction .84, induction .60. Exp 2: deduction .82, induction .71. Deduction curve farther from the origin in both. Deduction also more conservative.
limits: Unequal slopes can come from non-Gaussian strength distributions, a point Hayes et al. (2018) press.
agent_relevance: Collect confidence as well as the yes/no from any verifier we test; accept rate alone hides this.

source: Lassiter & Goodman (2012) How many kinds of reasoning? Inference, probability, and natural language semantics
finding: Rips and Rotello-Heit read the non-linear pattern as proof against probability-based single-scale theories. Lassiter and Goodman answer that the modal word (necessary, plausible) acts as a non-linear power function of conditional probability.
numbers: Model: P(yes) = P(C|P)^beta_M x (1 - eps) + eps/2, one beta per modal word; eps is the share of random responses; best-fit eps = .12. Implied threshold density p_M(theta) = beta * theta^(beta-1).
limits: A model of word meaning, not of a mental process.
agent_relevance: The question word is itself a parameter that bends accept rates. Our prompt wording will change accept rates in a predictable curved way with no change in thinking.

source: Lassiter & Goodman (2012) How many kinds of reasoning? Inference, probability, and natural language semantics
finding: A new within-subject paradigm changed only the modal word in the conclusion. The Heit-Rotello sensitivity gap was reproduced by a one-word change.
numbers: N=507 online, 485 native English speakers, 10,185 judgments, 21 arguments each from a pool of 63. Necessary: valid accepted .82, invalid .41, d'=1.15 +/- .19. Plausible: valid .94, invalid .82, d'=0.63 +/- .27; difference significant at p<.05. Rotello and Heit (2009) three-premise: deduction .94/.06, d' 3.31; induction .95/.17, d' 2.56.
limits: Online sample; invalid arguments accepted much more than in the lab (natural predicates invited guesses). Rips' crossover was not reproduced.
agent_relevance: The d' gap, a main evidence line for two processes, can be produced inside one task by changing a word. It is weak evidence for separate mental processes.

source: Lassiter & Goodman (2012) How many kinds of reasoning? Inference, probability, and natural language semantics
finding: Model fit: argument rank order should hold across modal frames. Fits came close to split-half reliability.
numbers: Fit R2 by modal: certain .60, likely .55, necessary .57, plausible .42, possible .32, probable .41 (split-half .66, .57, .70, .37, .34, .47). Mean Spearman rank correlation between frames .53 (model-simulated 95% range .49 to .64); permutation p<.0001.
limits: Beta values per modal read from figure captions; not all could be checked.
agent_relevance: Candidate ranking by strength should agree across a plausible prompt and a necessary prompt. Rank disagreement is a cheap signal that something other than strength is at work.

source: Lassiter & Goodman (2012) How many kinds of reasoning? Inference, probability, and natural language semantics
finding: Process story: people sample possible worlds and say yes only if the conclusion holds in every sample. Necessary needs more samples than plausible, so under time pressure necessary should look like plausible.
numbers: Authors link this to Heit and Rotello (2010), where speeded deduction looked like induction. They also explain the argument-length effect as more premises raising P(C|P).
limits: A proposed implementation, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: A validity check costs more samples than a plausibility check. With a small budget it degrades toward plausibility.

source: Hayes, Heit & Rotello (2014) Memory, reasoning, and categorization: parallels and common mechanisms
finding: Summary of Heit-Rotello signal detection work: argument length, similarity and typicality moved induction more than deduction; logical validity moved deduction more. Under time pressure deduction looked more like induction. A one-dimension model failed Monte Carlo fits; a two-dimension model fit.
numbers: d' differed between conditions; area under the ROC was larger for deduction; the two dimensions were roughly logical correctness and consistency with associative knowledge, weighted differently by instruction.
limits: Authors say it is premature to call the debate settled and cite Lassiter and Goodman (2012) and Stephens and Dunn (2013) as one-process rivals. Details in cited papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Two-cue picture: validity and plausibility are two signals and the instruction sets their weights. Practical use: request both signals and combine them in code.

source: Hayes, Heit & Rotello (2014) Memory, reasoning, and categorization: parallels and common mechanisms
finding: The interaction index used for belief bias for over 30 years is flawed, because it assumes a linear hit/false-alarm relation, like the corrected-recognition score in memory research.
numbers: Cites Dube et al. 2010, 2011 and Heit and Rotello 2014. In memory research the same single-versus-dual debate exists (familiarity and recollection).
limits: Review text; numbers sit in cited papers not opened here.
agent_relevance: Do not score a verifier with one difference score. Report hit and false-alarm rates or d'.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: Dissociations alone cannot prove two processes. One latent strength dimension mapped to answers by different monotonic functions can produce the same pattern, including double dissociations.
numbers: Cites Dunn and Kirsner (1988): double dissociations in recognition can arise from one latent variable. Rotello and Heit assumed identical Gaussian strength distributions for induction and deduction; Hayes et al. say there is no reason to assume that.
limits: Argument, not a data test; they do not claim Gaussian is wrong in fact.
agent_relevance: A prompt that changes accuracy on some item types and not others does not show two modules in the model.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: State-trace analysis plots mean induction endorsement against mean deduction endorsement over many conditions. If the points lie on one increasing curve, one latent dimension is enough; reliable departures need two or more.
numbers: Inference by conjoint monotonic regression (Kalish, Dunn, Burdakov and Sysoev 2016), 10,000 bootstrap samples, alpha .05. Sanity check: data simulated from a two-dimensional structure (30 per cell, 8 conditions) were rejected, statistic 12.78, p<.001.
limits: Needs the same items under both tasks and several conditions; the only assumption is monotonicity.
agent_relevance: A usable test for our own system: vary a factor over several levels and plot the validity-prompt score against the plausibility-prompt score.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: Experiment 1 (concurrent number-recall load and working-memory capacity): validity mattered more under deduction, believability more under induction, but the state-trace was monotonic.
numbers: N=122 undergraduates, 4 groups; 16 target items (modus ponens valid vs accepting the consequent invalid, x believable vs unbelievable). Validity x instruction chi2(1)=18.79; belief x instruction chi2(1)=13.64; both p<.001. Load had no effect (all p>=.14); recall .89 low load, .68 high load. Capacity x validity chi2(1)=28.30; three-way with instruction chi2(1)=6.23, p<.01. CMR tests: load p=.25, capacity p=.43.
limits: Only causal conditionals; load did not change reasoning, so a weak test.
agent_relevance: Low-capacity reasoners lean on belief especially when asked for plausibility. A small model asked for plausibility will lean on priors.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: Experiment 2 (verbal counting-backward load): same dissociation, again a single-dimension state-trace.
numbers: N=110 undergraduates; 106 in load analysis; WM groups n=55 each. Validity chi2(1)=205.69; validity x instruction chi2(1)=19.57, p<.001; belief x validity chi2(1)=15.51, p<.001; load effects all p>=.10.
limits: Load again interacted with nothing, so the manipulation may be too weak.
agent_relevance: Even heavy verbal load left the induction-deduction relation monotonic.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: Experiment 3 (decision time): speeding cut sensitivity to validity in both tasks; the state-trace across 24 conditions still fit one dimension.
numbers: N=122, 4 groups; 5.5 s deadline set where 80% of 20 unspeeded pilot participants were slower; prompt at 4 s; 16 targets plus 8 fillers. Null of one dimension retained in every CMR test (approximate CMR).
limits: Approximate CMR used for many points. Conclusions cover conditionals only.
agent_relevance: Time pressure removes validity discrimination for both prompts, not only for deduction.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning: Inductive and deductive inference can be explained by a single process
finding: The authors conclude that dissociations fit a common evidentiary scale for induction and deduction. They add limits: other factors may give two dimensions; syllogisms may recruit more analytic processing.
numbers: Quote: dissociations 'are consistent with a single-process model that assumes a common evidentiary scale for induction and deduction.'
limits: Only conditional arguments tested.
agent_relevance: Safe design assumption: one strength signal plus two cutoffs, until a stronger test shows otherwise.

source: Stephens, Dunn & Hayes (2018) Are there two processes in reasoning? The dimensionality of inductive and deductive inferences
finding: Signed difference analysis over many testable models on three data sets: nearly all rejected, including every 2-dimensional model. The only model fitting all three was one strength dimension with independent decision criteria for induction and deduction.
numbers: Based on an abstract and the description in Hayes et al. (2018): a review of 26 earlier studies, plus a new experiment where beliefs about base rates of valid and plausible items shifted the two criteria in opposite directions. Singmann and Klauer (2011) data challenged the fixed-criterion version.
limits: Psychological Review text not opened.
agent_relevance: Best current formal account: one signal, two independently movable thresholds. Base-rate expectations can shift a checker's cutoff.

source: Singmann, Klauer & Over (2014) New normative standards of conditional reasoning and the dual-source model
finding: Dual-source model (Klauer, Beller and Hutter 2010): a judgment mixes background-knowledge probability with the believed warrant of the logical form, weighted by one parameter. It is a mixing model, not two separate judgment systems.
numbers: Prediction = lambda*{tau(x) + (1-tau(x))*kappa(C,x)} + (1-lambda)*kappa(C,x); kappa is knowledge-based, tau form-based. 81% of 30 participants used form information (lambda>0), range .02 to .70, mean .31.
limits: German student sample; form component estimated from a separate abstract deductive task.
agent_relevance: A recipe for combining a does-the-form-guarantee-it signal with a does-it-fit-what-is-known signal in code.

source: Singmann, Klauer & Over (2014) New normative standards of conditional reasoning and the dual-source model
finding: The dual-source model, with the form part set from a deduction task and knowledge from probability estimates, predicted probabilized conditional inference as well as a model that used only the probability data.
numbers: N=30. Probabilized task: 16 conditionals, 4 per person, one inference each (MP, MT, AC, DA). Model effect F(2,50)=9.79, p<.001; dual-source vs BL model z=1.48, p=.14 (no difference); baseline worse, z=-4.17, p=.003. P(q|p) was the only unique predictor of P(if p then q).
limits: Small N; two sessions a week apart; believable conditionals only.
agent_relevance: Both kinds of information enter the same judgment.

source: Singmann, Klauer & Over (2014) New normative standards of conditional reasoning and the dual-source model
finding: Responses were confidence-preserving (p-valid) for modus ponens but not for modus tollens; coherence intervals beat chance for MP and, less so, DA.
numbers: 54% of participants gave too large P(q|not-p) estimates (scaling below 1); median scaling .95, mean 1.13, SD 1.18; three ignored it entirely.
limits: N=30; conclusions only for the inference types where intervals were computed.
agent_relevance: People respect validity for the easy form and drop it for the harder form. An agent should not trust its own validity sense on harder forms.

source: Evans, Thompson & Over (2015) Uncertain deduction and conditional reasoning
finding: When premises and conclusions get numeric probabilities and are grouped as an explicit inference, people respect probabilistic validity and coherence far better than when judging the same statements in separate tasks.
numbers: Hit rates in the Inference group on affirmative inferences (MP, AC): well over 80% for p-validity and about 75% for coherence. Belief group worse. Negative events harder.
limits: Exact N not extracted; hit rates only for affirmative forms.
agent_relevance: Showing premises and conclusion together improves the check. Put them side by side when asking for a validity-style check.

source: Evans, Thompson & Over (2015) Uncertain deduction and conditional reasoning
finding: The new paradigm drops assume-the-premises-true; norm is Bayesian (p-validity, coherence), with P(if p then q)=P(q|p). Validity becomes a bound on probability.
numbers: p-validity (Adams 1998): conclusion uncertainty cannot exceed the summed premise uncertainties. MP and MT are p-valid; AC and DA are not.
limits: Position paper plus one experiment; the Equation is not respected by every participant.
agent_relevance: Code check for valid forms: u(conclusion) <= u(premise 1) + u(premise 2).

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief: evidence for a parallel-processing model of belief bias
finding: Logic and belief signals run in parallel; which interferes depends on structural difficulty. Easy items (modus ponens): logic hurts belief judgments more; moderate: symmetric; hardest (three-term syllogisms): belief hurts logic judgments more.
numbers: Exp 1: conflict .68 vs no-conflict .92 (chi2(1)=39.7); MP conflict cost .30 for belief vs .24 for logic judgments, interaction chi2(1)=5.34, p=.02. MT symmetric. Exp 2 syllogisms: conflict .68 vs no-conflict .83; simple .80 vs complex .71. Power 81% for d=0.20 with 45 participants.
limits: Each participant did both belief and logic judgments in blocks; not a test of the single-dimension claim.
agent_relevance: On hard multi-step arguments expect belief to leak into the validity check; use code or a structured checker.

source: Hayes & Heit (2013) How similar are recognition memory and inductive reasoning?
finding: Recognition memory and induction fit one exemplar model (GEN-EX) of overall similarity under speeded judgments; unspeeded induction is shifted by property type.
numbers: N=140 undergraduates, 4 groups (recognition, induction blank, habitat, mammal); 10 study pictures at 1.5 s; 50 test items.
limits: Memory and induction, not deduction.
agent_relevance: Fast answers are driven by similarity; the same machinery gives different answers when the question changes.

source: Markovits (2024) Are there two kinds of reasoners?
finding: Dual-strategy view: individuals prefer counterexample (model-based) or statistical (probabilistic) reasoning; the choice shifts under time pressure and correlates with ability.
numbers: Diagnostic: two sets of five affirming-the-consequent inferences with about 90% vs 50% P&Q frequency over 1000 observations. Counterexample reasoners reject all; statistical reasoners follow frequencies. Under time pressure reasoners moved toward statistical answers (Markovits et al. 2013). Counterexample reasoners score higher on IQ, CRT and AOT.
limits: Author's own review; covered by subfield 07, so only noted here.
agent_relevance: No fixed mode is needed: pick strategy by problem and by budget.
